title: Pho Bo
subtitle: Vietnamese beef noodle soup with charred ginger and spices
excerpt: Vietnam's national soup: a clear, fragrant beef broth deeply scented with charred ginger and onion, star anise, cinnamon, and clove, poured boiling over thin rice noodles and wafer-thin slices of raw beef that cook in the bowl.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pho (pronounced approximately as 'fuh') is the defining dish of Vietnamese cooking and particularly associated with Hanoi, where it originated in the early twentieth century as a street food. The word may derive from the French pot-au-feu, introduced during the colonial era, though Vietnamese culinary historians dispute this. The soup consists of three separate elements: the broth, which requires hours of careful cooking from beef bones with charred aromatics and whole spices; the noodles; and the toppings, which are added raw at the table. The broth is the thing: without a rich, clear, deeply flavoured stock, pho is nothing. It must be skimmed and strained to clarity. The charring of the ginger and onion directly over a flame gives the broth its distinctive sweet, slightly smoky depth.

content.text: Blanch the bones in boiling water for 5 minutes and rinse before making the broth; this removes impurities that would cloud the soup. Char the ginger and onion directly over a gas flame or under a hot grill until blackened in patches; do not skip this step. Keep the broth at a very gentle simmer throughout.

items.preparation: for the broth; removed after cooking and sliced to serve
good beef stock; or water if making from bones
a large piece; charred directly over a flame until blackened
halved; charred cut-side down until blackened
flat, thin rice noodles; soaked in cold water for 30 minutes
raw; sliced paper-thin across the grain; for serving in the bowl

content.text: Put the blanched bones and brisket in a large pot. Cover with 3 litres of cold water and bring slowly to a simmer. Skim the surface carefully. Add the charred ginger, charred onion, star anise, cinnamon, cloves, and coriander seeds. Simmer gently, uncovered, for 3 hours.

Remove the brisket after 2 hours (it should be tender); slice and set aside. Continue simmering the broth for the remaining time. Strain through a fine sieve. Season with fish sauce, sugar, and salt. The broth should be clear, fragrant, and deeply savoury.

Cook the soaked rice noodles in boiling water for 1 to 2 minutes until just tender; drain. Divide between 4 large bowls. Lay the raw beef slices and some brisket slices on top. Pour the boiling broth over immediately; the raw beef will cook in the heat of the broth. Top with spring onions, coriander, and beansprouts. Serve with lime wedges and chilli.
